newsitem.title: USA: NYS speaker details conditions for LIPA pact.
newsitem.headline: NYS speaker details conditions for LIPA pact.

text.p: The New York Assembly Speaker Tuesday set out the conditions under which he would approve Governor George Pataki's plan to cut Long Island's electricity rates with the nation's biggest-ever tax-exempt bond sale.

Pataki wants the Long Island Power Authority (LIPA) to sell $7.3 billion of tax-exempt bonds and use the money to buy assets from the Long Island Lighting Co and Brooklyn Union Gas, which plan to merge.
The governor said he expected the Speaker's conditions to be met by Wednesday, when the state board that approves tax-exempt borrowings was expected to vote on the pact.
The Speaker, Sheldon Silver, D-Manhattan, along with Pataki and Senate Majority Leader Joseph Bruno, R-Troy, holds veto power over the board's decisions.
The following list highlights recommendations made by Silver in appendices to a letter to Pataki.

--Before selling debt and no later than one year after the Public Authorities Control Board approves the pact, LIPA must adopt a resolution with a clear timetable for open access to its distribution system, so all customers would be able to pick other power suppliers within 10 years.

If LIPA bought LILCO's fossil fuel plants, it would have to then sell its generation facilities, unless such a sale were not financially sound or the facility was needed to meet the Authority's obligation to be the provider of last resort.
The utility's workforce would have to be protected against "unfair impacts" of the transition.
--The price of LILCO generation facilities cannot exceed book value at the time of purchase.
--LILCO and Brooklyn Union must invest in energy-related economic development in Nassau, Suffolk and Queens, including natural gas infrastructure improvements.

Silver estimated LILCO and Brooklyn Union would get $1.9 billion from the deal. He said the two utilities had testified they would have to invest the money in energy-related activities to avoid federal taxes on recouping accelerated depreciation of LILCO's Shoreham nuclear plant.

"This investment will also provide a real source of competition without technology changes in the transmission of electricity," said Silver, adding that in Brooklyn the percentage of homes using natural gas was over 77 percent, but only about 27 percent in LILCO's service area.
--LIPA, LILCO and Brooklyn Union must guarantee an average rate reduction, calculated against current rates, for the first 10 years of the deal.

--LIPA cannot have complete control over its own rate setting. Any rise in LIPA's rates that exceeded 2-1/2 percent over a one-year period would have to be approved by the Public Service Commission and be subject to hearings.
